nodes.description: Standard focal-epilepsy pharmacotherapy is the first thing tried and, in this disorder, usually the thing that fails. Drug resistance is close to definitional in the surgical series that define FCD type II, since those are the patients who reach a surgical centre, and it is the reason the treatment section here is dominated by resection rather than by drugs. No antiseizure medication is specifically indicated for FCD type II or acts on the mTOR mechanism; the agent listed is representative of the class rather than a targeted therapy.

evidence.reference_title: Focal Cortical Dysplasia: Gene Mutations, Cell Signaling, and Therapeutic Implications.
evidence.snippet: Focal cortical dysplasias (FCDs) are malformations of cortical development (MCDs) that are highly associated with medication-resistant epilepsy and are the most common cause of neocortical epilepsy in children.

evidence.reference_title: Clinical features and surgical outcomes in young children with focal cortical dysplasia type II.
evidence.snippet: Young children (onset age ≤6 years) with FCDII who underwent epileptic surgery in Children Epilepsy Center of Peking University First Hospital in 2014-2018 were followed up for at least 6 months after surgery.

nodes.description: Whichever gene is hit, the convergent consequence is unrestrained mTORC1 activity in the mutant clone, read out histologically as strong phospho-S6 ribosomal protein immunostaining. This convergence is why FCD type II behaves as one disease despite a heterogeneous gene list, and why cases in which no variant is found are still classified as mTORopathies.

nodes.description: The mTOR pathway governs neuronal growth and migration, so the mutant clone fails to laminate normally. The result is loss of the normal six-layer cortical architecture with abnormal cellular polarity, the histological substrate of the radiological blurring of the grey-white junction.

evidence.reference_title: Focal Cortical Dysplasia: Gene Mutations, Cell Signaling, and Therapeutic Implications.
evidence.snippet: Focal cortical dysplasias (FCDs) are malformations of cortical development (MCDs) that are highly associated with medication-resistant epilepsy and are the most common cause of neocortical epilepsy in children.

nodes.description: mTORC1 drives cell growth, so mutant cells become cytomegalic. Dysmorphic neurons are enlarged, abnormally oriented neurons with aberrant neurofilament accumulation. Balloon cells, which define subtype IIb, are large cells with opalescent cytoplasm that can co-express neuronal and glial progenitor markers. Both cell populations carry the pathogenic variant. Whether balloon cells actually generate seizures is contested and is recorded as a discussion.

evidence.snippet: These abnormal cells emerge during early brain development as a result of a hyperactive mTOR pathway and may express both neuronal and glial markers.

nodes.description: An mTORC1 inhibitor, mechanistically the obvious targeted therapy for a mosaic mTORopathy. A randomized crossover placebo-controlled trial in FCD type 2 did not show overall superiority over placebo, although the small number of patients who did become seizure-free carried MTOR variants or had no identified variant. Mucositis and skin ulceration were common. The gap between the mechanistic rationale and the trial result is recorded as a discussion.

evidence.reference_title: Efficacy and safety of everolimus for patients with focal cortical dysplasia type 2.
evidence.snippet: There was no significant difference in the primary outcome between everolimus and placebo groups (24% vs. 19%, p = 0.66).

evidence.reference_title: Efficacy and safety of everolimus for patients with focal cortical dysplasia type 2.
evidence.snippet: Three patients with a pathogenic variant in the MTOR gene or no genetic abnormalities achieved seizure freedom with everolimus in the last month of the core phase, while none of the patients with variants in other genes did.

evidence.reference_title: Efficacy and safety of everolimus for patients with focal cortical dysplasia type 2.

nodes.description: The dysplastic patch generates epileptiform activity intrinsically rather than merely irritating adjacent normal cortex. Mouse work titrating the mosaic burden shows a remarkably low threshold: a few thousand mutation-bearing neurons, well under a tenth of a percent of cells, suffice to produce spontaneous seizures, and the burden scales with seizure frequency and onset.

evidence.reference_title: Threshold of somatic mosaicism leading to brain dysfunction with focal epilepsy.
evidence.snippet: approximately 8000-9000 neurons expressing the MTOR mutant, extrapolated to constitute 0.08%-0.09% of total cells or roughly 0.04% of variant allele frequency in the mouse hemicortex, were sufficient to trigger epileptic seizures

evidence.reference_title: Threshold of somatic mosaicism leading to brain dysfunction with focal epilepsy.
evidence.snippet: The mutational burden was correlated with seizure frequency and onset

nodes.description: Surgical removal of the dysplastic cortex is the definitive treatment and the only intervention that reliably produces seizure freedom. Outcome is driven by completeness of resection, which is why the practical difficulty is delineating lesion boundaries, particularly in the substantial minority of MRI-occult lesions. In a large pediatric FCD surgical cohort complete seizure control was achieved in roughly half of patients and was durable over years.

evidence.reference_title: Long-term seizure outcome in pediatric patients with focal cortical dysplasia undergoing tailored and standard surgical resections.
evidence.snippet: Complete seizure control (Engel Ia) was achieved in 56% after two years, 52% at five years, and 50% at last follow-up

nodes.description: The other mTOR inhibitor tried in this disorder, in the FCDS-01 study of 16 patients aged 6 to 57. Focal seizure frequency fell by 25 percent overall with a 33 percent response rate, but the reduction did not reach the predetermined level of statistical significance and the external control comparison was confounded by differing baseline characteristics. Taken together with the negative everolimus trial, this is a second independent failure of systemic mTOR inhibition to clear a prespecified bar in FCD type II, which is why the associated discussion treats the strategy as unestablished rather than merely under-tested.

evidence.reference_title: Sirolimus for epileptic seizures associated with focal cortical dysplasia type II.
evidence.snippet: The reduction of focal seizures did not meet the predetermined level of statistical significance.

evidence.reference_title: Sirolimus for epileptic seizures associated with focal cortical dysplasia type II.
evidence.snippet: The focal seizure frequency reduced by 25% in all patients during the maintenance therapy period and by a median value of 17%, 28%, and 23% during the 1-4-, 5-8-, and 9-12-week periods. The response rate was 33%.

nodes.description: A post-zygotic variant arises in a neural progenitor during corticogenesis, either a gain-of-function change in an mTORC1 activator (MTOR itself, or AKT3, PIK3CA, RHEB) or loss of function in an mTORC1 repressor (DEPDC5, NPRL3 and the other GATOR1 components, or TSC1/TSC2). Because the variant is confined to the descendants of that one progenitor, it is present only in the affected patch of brain and is typically undetectable in blood. Repressor cases frequently require a germline first hit plus a somatic second hit in the lesion.
nodes.id: Somatic mTOR Pathway Variant in a Cortical Progenitor

evidence.reference_title: Dissecting the genetic basis of focal cortical dysplasia: a large cohort study.
evidence.snippet: Somatic gain-of-function variants in MTOR and its activators (AKT3, PIK3CA, RHEB), as well as germline, somatic and two-hit loss-of-function variants in its repressors (DEPDC5, TSC1, TSC2) were found exclusively in FCD2/HME cases.

evidence.reference_title: Dissecting the genetic basis of focal cortical dysplasia: a large cohort study.
evidence.snippet: Single-cell microdissection followed by sequencing of enriched pools of DNs unveiled a somatic second-hit loss-of-heterozygosity in a DEPDC5 germline case.
